- Model consistently underestimates prices in early periods (first 10–15 days) and overestimates in late periods (last 10–15 days), suggesting a lag or asymmetric response to recent trends.
- Forecasts tend to overshoot after sharp price spikes (e.g., 80+ → 85+), then correct downward — indicate overreaction to volatility.
- Mean reversion is evident: forecasts often drift toward historical averages (e.g., 70–75 range) after initial overestimation, but not always fast enough.
- Model exhibits persistent downward bias in the 70–75 range, especially when history is stable — may be underweighting demand or supply shocks.
- When history includes a recent high (e.g., 80+), forecasts often fail to capture the full magnitude of the high, underestimating the true peak.
- Forecasts are overly sensitive to short-term volatility — may be overfitting recent noise rather than underlying trends.
- Model tends to underestimate the true value when the 30-day history is trending upward — may be missing momentum or policy-driven price support.
- When true outcome is near historical mean, model often predicts slightly below — may be underestimating baseline support or missing seasonal factors.
- Forecasts show a tendency to “smooth” sharp declines — may be underreacting to supply shocks or policy changes.
- Model often overestimates the “recovery” phase after a dip — may be overconfident in rebound potential without sufficient context.
